narrative:
Your application was denied because the model estimated a 51.0% probability that you would fail the bar exam on the first attempt. That is only slightly above a coin flip, but it means the model judged failure to be marginally more likely than passing, which was enough to place your file in the rejected group.

The strongest factor behind that judgment was your third-year class standing. You were in the first decile, while accepted students averaged around the sixth decile. This very low third-year rank was the main feature pushing the prediction toward bar exam failure. Your undergraduate GPA of 3.70 was the second most influential factor, and it pushed toward passing because it is above the accepted-student average of about 3.23. Your LSAT score of 34 was the third most influential factor. Although it is below the accepted average of about 37.18, in the context of your full file it was treated as a positive factor rather than the main reason for rejection.

What should you do next? Focus on the issue the model weighted most heavily: your third-year academic record. If there were special circumstances, document them and show any later evidence of stronger performance. Consider retaking the LSAT if you can improve your score, and seek admissions counseling about whether to appeal, take additional coursework, or apply again after strengthening the part of your record that drove the denial.
